segments.title: What the Royal Navy expected war games to teach
segments.body: The Admiralty's Tactical Division issued a common framework that could be used from individual-ship drills through fleet exercises. The manual separated cruiser problems, strategical exercises, mining and minesweeping, aviation, and communications. Strategical was the broader period term, although strategic later became standard. Its stated goals included teaching the battle plan, building common tactical doctrine, testing new ideas and material, and encouraging subordinate initiative. Officers also had to learn the capabilities of foreign ships and apply realistic navigation errors to aircraft operating as independent formations. War might begin anywhere and bring together ships from different stations at short notice, so shared methods were essential to making an improvised force work together. The rules linked tabletop decisions, staff training, and practical fleet exercises into one system of readiness.

evidence.note: The transcript introduces ADM 186/78, its authorship, scope, and tactical training objectives.

segments.summary: The 1929 rules connected tabletop decisions to fleet exercises, common doctrine, decentralized command, and readiness for a war that might begin anywhere.

segments.title: War games made damage assessment part of officer education
segments.body: Damage umpires used chips to record the consequences of torpedo attacks while still making the weapon dangerous enough to force realistic deployment decisions. The same rules could be used at Greenwich, on flag staffs, aboard larger ships, or by destroyer flotillas working from depot ships and shore. Officers of different substantive ranks could be given exercise commands above their ordinary standing, so the game tested judgment and made its decisions visible to umpires. The service also encouraged historical reading as part of professional development. Wargaming was a distributed school for command in which the result was only one part of the lesson.

evidence.note: The transcript connects torpedo adjudication, damage chips, shore and fleet games, temporary commands, and historical reading to officer training.

segments.summary: Damage chips, distributed fleet play, temporary exercise commands, and professional reading made wargaming a practical school for naval judgment.

segments.title: Cruiser problems disguised the practice of economic war
segments.body: The politically awkward subject of surface raiding could be taught under the safer label of a cruiser problem. Exercise rules demanded realistic movements, fuel and endurance calculations, accurate plotting of friendly forces, disciplined command relationships, and written narratives. Junior officers could temporarily receive senior game commands, forcing everyone to respect the exercise chain of command and giving promising officers a demanding test. This attention to staff work and reporting reflected the Royal Navy's effort to prevent another breakdown like the communication failures at Jutland. An apparently tactical game also rehearsed the administrative habits needed to command at sea.

evidence.note: The transcript explains cruiser problems, chart work, command roles, Jutland, and exercise narratives.

segments.summary: Cruiser exercises trained scouting, patrol, and commerce-war skills while also rehearsing chart work, communications, command relationships, and war diaries.

segments.title: Gunnery tables turned peacetime results into battle estimates
segments.body: The rules began with Royal Navy firing practice from 1922 to 1926 and cut the recorded hit rate by 30 percent to approximate action conditions. Umpires then modified the result for target size, smoke, visibility, air spotting, and whether the firing ship was under return fire. Separate entries allowed different battleship types and gun arrangements to be compared within the same problem. The arbitrary reduction may have undervalued trained gunners, but it kept exercises from treating peacetime accuracy as a wartime guarantee. The resulting table modeled uncertainty and combat friction instead of predicting results from one headline percentage.

evidence.note: The transcript explains the 30 percent action-condition discount and the target, visibility, smoke, air-spotting, and return-fire factors.

segments.summary: The rules discounted peacetime accuracy, then layered target size, smoke, visibility, air spotting, and return fire into an estimate of wartime gunnery.

segments.title: The tables preserved speculative designs and an evolving destroyer role
segments.body: The hitting tables give the Queen Elizabeth class both 15-inch and 16-inch figures. The dual figures may show that the class served as a baseline for other designs under consideration. The same pages still use the older torpedo-boat-destroyer description for W-class ships. By 1929, destroyers were increasingly expected to conduct independent operations and attack heavier forces themselves. The terminology had not yet caught up fully with the role, while the staff also used the broad label heavy ships for capital units. This technical manual preserves unbuilt design choices and a change in naval classification that a battle narrative could easily miss.

evidence.note: The transcript discusses a 16-inch Queen Elizabeth option, the W-class torpedo-boat-destroyer label, changing destroyer employment, and heavy-ship terminology.

segments.summary: A 16-inch Queen Elizabeth alternative and the fading torpedo-boat-destroyer label show the rulebook capturing both unbuilt ideas and changing ship roles.

segments.title: Cumulative damage and speed loss changed how a fleet could fight
segments.body: The tables accumulated non-vital 15-inch hits differently for older and newer battleships, so many hits could erode fighting power before a ship was treated as destroyed. They also included the Lewis gun and 3-inch anti-aircraft weapons then in service and pointed toward the imminent move to the 4-inch high-angle gun. Torpedo allowances began from official outfit figures, even though destroyers might carry extra weapons in wartime. After deciding the number of hits, an umpire imposed either a speed reduction or a loss of fighting efficiency. The penalties had different operational effects: speed loss constrained formation maneuver, while reduced fighting efficiency cut combat power in the next engagement. The model treated damage as an operational problem rather than simple hull survival.

evidence.note: The transcript covers cumulative non-vital hits, period anti-aircraft guns, official and wartime torpedo loads, and speed versus fighting-efficiency penalties.

segments.summary: Non-vital hits, early anti-aircraft weapons, torpedo outfits, and separate speed and fighting-efficiency penalties made damage operational rather than binary.

segments.title: Warhead size and hit location determined torpedo consequences
segments.body: Tables distinguished 750-pound, 500-pound, and 320-pound explosive charges and estimated how many hits different ship types might absorb. The discussion questions whether Nelson could remain afloat after six of the heaviest hits, a reminder that the exercise rules rested on explicit assumptions rather than observed wartime results. The location of a hit could matter as much as the nominal warhead. Damage to rudders, shafts, or propellers threatened maneuver and could reduce the speed of the entire formation. Naval wargaming translated weapon characteristics into consequences for the whole fleet.

evidence.note: The transcript compares three torpedo explosive charges, questions the Nelson-class allowance, and explains the importance of rudder, shaft, and propeller hits.

segments.summary: Warhead weight and damage to rudders, shafts, or propellers translated an individual torpedo hit into consequences for the whole formation.

segments.title: Periscope visibility and serviceability constrained reconnaissance
segments.body: Submarine visibility tables varied the distance at which ships and destroyers could be seen through a periscope according to sea state and the proximity of the enemy. The model forced officers to consider how long and how high a periscope could safely be exposed. Aircraft calculations began with 90 percent serviceability, fell to 80 percent on the second day, and used 70 percent thereafter during sustained operations. Worked examples converted those percentages into the number of floatplanes that could remain continuously aloft. Reconnaissance depended on equipment availability, observation conditions, and endurance.

evidence.note: The transcript explains periscope visibility ranges and declining aircraft serviceability during sustained operations.

segments.summary: The rules treated submarine sighting distance and the declining serviceability of aircraft as operational limits rather than abstract background details.

segments.title: Carrier deck capacity turned fleet aviation into a timing problem
segments.body: The rules specified how many large aircraft, fighters, or reconnaissance machines each British carrier could range on its decks. Lift arrangements and hangar position changed the time needed to bring aircraft up, while water-cooled and radial engines required different warm-up allowances. Foreign carriers were mapped to British comparison types: Hosho to Hermes, and Kaga, Lexington, and Saratoga to Furious. The rules even credited the American carriers with the ability to range aircraft forward while preserving landing space aft. Carrier strength depended on air-group size and the tempo at which a ship could launch and recover its aircraft.

evidence.note: The transcript lists British deck capacities, foreign-carrier comparison types, lift timings, and engine warm-up allowances.

segments.summary: Deck space, lifts, hangars, engine warm-up, and foreign carrier comparisons determined how quickly an air group could become a usable striking force.

segments.title: Air attack tables connected weapons effects to operational range
segments.body: The rules estimated aerial torpedo hits by formation size, target type, maneuver, and the possibility of surprise. Battleships and carriers were more suitable targets than cruisers or destroyers, while bombing tables sharply reduced an aircraft's chance of damaging a deeply submerged submarine. Radius of action meant the greatest straight-line distance an aircraft could fly while retaining enough fuel to return, not its theoretical maximum range. Fuel capacity, airspeed, time over the objective, wind, launch delays, landing delays, and emergency reserves all entered the calculation. This complexity gave more officers realistic work and connected a local fleet exercise to the demands of a wider war. The damage model also encouraged carrier aircraft to slow enemy formations so the battle fleet could bring them to action.

evidence.note: The transcript covers aerial torpedo probabilities, bombing against submarines, radius of action, fuel margins, and formation-speed damage.

segments.summary: Torpedo-hit probabilities, bombing depth limits, fuel reserves, wind, and recovery delays made naval air strikes a combined weapons-and-endurance calculation.

segments.title: Communications rules prepared fleets for dispersed warfare
segments.body: Wireless messages were assigned realistic transmission times that grew with traffic and priority demands. Maneuver signals, first contact reports, later reports, and outgoing admiral's signals could therefore reach recipients at different speeds. The Royal Navy was anticipating combat dispersed both globally and tactically, with aviation extending the battlefield and darkness increasing uncertainty. Staffs had to decide what deserved priority while avoiding congestion that could delay a commander's plan. Repeated practice helped officers exchange necessary information under pressure, even if wartime signals would never be perfect or instantaneous.

evidence.note: The transcript explains wireless timing, traffic priority, dispersed action, night-fighting complexity, and the resulting wartime practice.

segments.summary: Signal delays and traffic priorities were built into games because carriers and night operations were spreading actions across much wider areas.

segments.title: Exercise MZ tested air attack in a balanced fleet problem
segments.body: MZ pitted the Mediterranean and Atlantic Fleets against one another, with ships representing additional battleships and battlecruisers that were not physically present. The stronger red force may approximate a likely Royal Navy task group, while the blue force may represent a Japanese opponent, although British battlecruisers stood in for foreign fast heavy ships. Both sides fielded carriers, submarines, reconnaissance aircraft, fighters, and torpedo bombers. Ten aircraft from Courageous were assessed to hit Nelson twice and Rodney once, reducing the squadron to eleven knots. Because the March exercise used an early copy of the rules published in April, it also acted as a practical test of the damage model before final issue.

evidence.note: The transcript introduces MZ's represented forces, possible Japanese comparison, carrier aircraft, and assessed attacks on Nelson and Rodney.

segments.summary: Exercise MZ matched carrier-supported fleets in a Mediterranean problem and used the new rules to translate air attacks into lost battle-fleet speed.

segments.title: Air reconnaissance freed cruisers but exposed the carriers
segments.body: Frobisher was put out of action while confirming an air report that had already located the enemy battle fleet. The exercise report asked whether cruisers could instead attack carriers, dominate the area ahead of the fleet, support friendly carriers, or strike destroyer flotillas. This new freedom also revealed that the destroyers near a carrier were often plane guards rather than a security screen capable of stopping hostile cruisers. The lesson anticipated the danger later demonstrated by the wartime losses of Courageous and Glorious when operational circumstances left them inadequately protected. MZ also criticized the dispersal of surface and aerial torpedo attacks across too many objectives.

evidence.note: The transcript discusses Frobisher, alternative cruiser tasks, carrier vulnerability, and dispersed surface and aerial torpedo attacks.

segments.summary: MZ showed that aircraft could replace cruiser scouting, allowing cruisers to raid the enemy screen or carriers while exposing the weakness of carrier protection.

segments.title: Mediterranean exercises combined training, presence, and Far East access
segments.body: The MZ exercise area around Corsica, Sardinia, and Algiers offered more predictable weather than the Atlantic, allowing complex fleet training with fewer weather interruptions. Maneuvering there also demonstrated British naval strength to Italy, Spain, France, and other regional observers. The Mediterranean was the route the Royal Navy would have to use to reinforce the Far East, so crews needed to know its waters and be prepared for interference while in transit. A worst-case planning example imagined an Italian-Japanese alignment threatening a Pacific-bound fleet in transit. The exercise geography supported training, deterrent presence, and global reinforcement planning at the same time.

evidence.note: The transcript links Mediterranean weather, naval presence, regional signalling, water familiarity, and the reinforcement route to the Far East.

segments.summary: The exercise area offered reliable training weather, demonstrated British strength, and rehearsed movement along the route a fleet would use to reinforce the Far East.

segments.title: Exercise M1 tested concentrated carrier torpedo strikes
segments.body: M1 brought together Blackburn Dart torpedo bombers, Fairey IIIF and IIID reconnaissance aircraft, Fairey Flycatcher fighters, and a Blackburn Bison alongside carriers with different normal speeds. Flying operations required the carriers to accelerate to about twenty-five knots, making their movement part of the tactical problem. The report endorsed the earliest possible warning of hostile surface forces and considered dedicated aircraft for that purpose. It also made senior officers across the fleet responsible for knowing the carriers' position and heading off enemy forces trying to work around the battle line. Air fighting in MZ encouraged further experiments with fighter patrols over the fleet, so carrier defense was becoming a combined responsibility rather than a matter for the carrier alone.

evidence.note: The transcript describes M1's aircraft, carrier speed for flight operations, early warning, carrier security, and fighter patrols.

segments.summary: Exercise M1 linked the speed needed for flying operations to early warning, fighter patrols, and the duty of the whole fleet to protect its carriers.

segments.title: M1 linked carrier command, torpedo performance, and strike concentration
segments.body: With no dedicated Rear Admiral Aircraft Carriers in 1929, the senior carrier remarks came through the vice admiral commanding the battlecruiser squadron, placing the technical debate inside a fast-force command structure. Short-range torpedo aiming depended heavily on pilot judgment, while differences in torpedo reliability and practice helped explain the contrasting results of the Mediterranean and Atlantic Fleets. Senior officers argued that a concerted attack by all available torpedo bombers should be more effective than separate attacks from each carrier. Concentration, however, imposed a delay and became harder to control at night, when several smaller formations might be more manageable than one mass. The exercise also tested how many fighters should remain over the fleet and how many should escort the striking force. Some officers expected the rear guns of two-seat torpedo bombers to reduce the need for fighter protection, revealing a doctrinal assumption that later combat would challenge.

evidence.note: The transcript compares carrier command, torpedo sights, weapon reliability, pilot practice, massed attacks, night control, and fighter escort.

segments.summary: M1 exposed the carriers' place under battlecruiser command while weighing torpedo reliability, pilot practice, fighter escort, and the delay needed to combine several air groups.

segments.title: Exercise OA tested mixed battle fleets and divided screens
segments.body: OA began with a Gibraltar relief setting and asked how a battleship force should fight an opponent mixing battleships and battlecruisers. It also tested whether destroyer flotillas should be divided into groups on each wing of the approaching battle fleet. Cardiff, Caledon, Vindictive, and Comus fought under heavy pressure while the Third Cruiser Squadron lost its bearing on the battle fleet. Once the danger from submarines seemed to have passed, the destroyers moved into wing positions for their attack. A reported downed reconnaissance aircraft drew Argus and the First Flotilla away to rescue the aircrew and salvage the machine. Neither could rejoin before the action, showing how an essential rescue could abruptly change the force available for a planned battle.

evidence.note: The transcript sets out OA's Gibraltar scenario, mixed heavy forces, destroyer-wing experiment, cruiser action, and rescue diversion.

segments.summary: OA tested a mixed battleship-and-battlecruiser force, divided destroyer screens, and the disruption caused when rescue duties removed ships from the battle.

segments.title: K26 obeyed its target priority and passed up Hood
segments.body: K26 reached a position from which it could have fired at Hood from about 3,500 yards. The submarine did not attack because its orders prioritized the enemy battle fleet. It then had to dive to eighty feet as Hood closed and took no further part in the exercise. The episode exposed the cost of rigid target priorities when an unexpected high-value opportunity appeared, while also showing the discipline required to pursue an assigned fleet objective. Because the claimed destruction of Hood was an exercise judgment rather than an observed attack, the learning value lies in the command decision and lost opportunity rather than a certain combat result.

evidence.note: The transcript follows K26's close opportunity against Hood, its target-priority decision, deep dive, and loss of further participation.

segments.summary: OA's most striking command problem came when K26 declined a close shot at Hood because its assigned objective was the enemy battle fleet.

segments.title: OA's battle result made victory a costly operational state
segments.body: The surface action was fought in an exercise band of about 13,000 to 15,000 yards. At this anticipated range, the higher volume of a 6-inch cruiser battery could be preferable to an 8-inch battery. Rodney and the represented ships of the Third Battle Squadron also fired torpedoes, although maneuver was expected to make some tracks pass ahead of Red. The damage model cut Blue to thirteen knots and assessed Nelson and Rodney at fifty percent out of action before the final reckoning. Blue then lost or effectively lost its battlecruisers and much of its battle line, yet Red's surviving battleships were also slowed and heavily damaged. Calling Red the winner hides how little usable force remained after the exercise. The game measured combat power, formation speed, and follow-on capability instead of reducing the engagement to a binary result.

evidence.note: The transcript covers the engagement range, 6-inch versus 8-inch cruiser argument, capital-ship torpedoes, speed loss, damage assessments, and Red's costly victory.

segments.summary: Exercise ranges, capital-ship torpedo fire, speed loss, and accumulated damage left Red the nominal winner but with little unhampered force remaining.

segments.title: Submarines overloaded the fleet before they scored a hit
segments.body: The exercise logged 78 flying hours and 34 deck landings while tracking reconnaissance, fighter, and torpedo-bomber strength, forced landings, and sortie duration. Argus carried spotter-reconnaissance aircraft and fighters but no torpedo bombers, an allocation that helps explain the later appeal of the Fairey Swordfish. Eagle maintained a continuous anti-submarine patrol, showing that submarine pressure consumed air effort even before a successful attack. The Admiralty concluded that fleet submarines forced aircraft and light forces away from their main tasks, congested communications, complicated the withdrawal of the ASW screen, and could delay a favorable attack. They also threatened to reduce battle-fleet speed or damage valuable advanced units such as battlecruisers and carriers. Together, the reports and competing dangers created operational overload for any commander without a staff able to filter and act on them.

evidence.note: The transcript gives OA's air activity and Admiralty conclusions about submarine-driven diversion, congestion, delay, and speed loss.

segments.summary: OA measured sustained flying and ASW patrols, then concluded that submarine pressure could divert forces, congest signals, and delay a fleet commander's decisions.

segments.title: Exercise OD rehearsed convoy interception and night battle
segments.body: OD gave a weaker but faster force the task of attacking a protected convoy while avoiding the enemy's superior battle strength. The scenario placed bases at Malta and Port Said and made Derna an advanced base under siege by red land forces. Blue submarine attacks on red communications had left the besieging army urgently short of reinforcements and stores, so the convoy's passage had a direct effect ashore. Ships represented absent battlecruisers and other units, allowing the exercise to model a larger operational force than the fleet physically available. The open-ended format let the commander-in-chief continue the problem until the participants had extracted its useful lessons. The commander-in-chief controlled Red but allowed Blue's plan to continue instead of ending the contest at a convenient point for his own side.

evidence.note: The transcript lays out OD's forces, protected-convoy problem, Derna supply crisis, open-ended format, and the controller's decision to let Blue continue.

segments.summary: OD embedded a protected convoy in a Mediterranean land campaign, linking submarine attacks on communications to the urgent need for reinforcements and stores at Derna.

segments.title: OD used air search to set up a night interception
segments.body: Blue spread submarines toward Malta and ordered Courageous to search up to eighty miles while maintaining visual contact with the battlecruiser Revenge. Once the convoy was located, aircraft and submarines were to shadow it and help the faster force avoid a superior opponent in daylight. The intended solution was a night attack, drawing on the lesson of Jutland that darkness could help a weaker force escape or reverse a numerical disadvantage. The exercise produced complicated night encounters involving battlecruisers and destroyers between 00:30 and 02:20. Its conclusions called for continued heavy-ship night training and a reliable system of recognition signals, because tactical aggression was useless if formations could not identify one another after dark.

evidence.note: The transcript describes Blue's air and submarine search, daylight avoidance, night encounters, and recognition-signal lesson.

segments.summary: Blue planned to locate and shadow the convoy with aircraft and submarines, refuse battle by day, and use darkness to offset the enemy's superior strength.

segments.title: Exercise OC linked submarine shadowing with air and ASW screens
segments.body: OC used L-class submarines to represent a G-class flotilla operating from Philippeville. Intelligence about a damaged battlecruiser drew the opposing fleet to sea, giving the submarines an opportunity to form an interception line. Their orders were to locate, shadow, and report the fleet so Red could bring it to action rather than merely attack whatever appeared first. Courageous and its attendant destroyers operated with the battle squadron, making air cooperation and carrier positioning part of the same reconnaissance problem. Submarines served as fleet scouts and information providers alongside their role as torpedo attackers.

evidence.note: The transcript describes OC's represented submarine flotilla, intelligence scenario, interception line, shadowing orders, and carrier-supported battle squadron.

segments.summary: OC asked a submarine line to intercept, shadow, and report a fleet so another force could bring it to action.

segments.title: OC opened a wider problem of air-ASW cooperation
segments.body: The commanding officer of Courageous proposed combining spotter-reconnaissance aircraft with destroyers to prevent submarines from maintaining contact. A night sweep followed by a bold change of course might break the shadowing line, while further trials could compare destroyer groups operating with and without aircraft. The discussion expanded into coordination between aircraft and ASDIC vessels, emergency procedures for forced landings near submarines, and whether a carrier could maneuver safely in the triangle behind the screen. Senior officers disagreed about what could be tested without endangering submarines or distorting the exercise, and the commander-in-chief warned against drawing universal conclusions from a carefully arranged set piece. The Royal Navy responded to the growing complexity of carrier employment by creating the Rear Admiral Aircraft Carriers appointment in 1930, filled by former Furious commander Reginald Henderson.

evidence.note: The transcript debates aircraft-destroyer cooperation, night contact-breaking, ASDIC screens, carrier safety, exercise limits, and carrier command.

segments.summary: Debate after OC explored aircraft-guided destroyer sweeps, breaking submarine contact at night, and the carrier's safe place behind an ASDIC screen.

segments.title: The 1929 exercises found questions faster than answers
segments.body: The Royal Navy was synthesizing lessons from the 1920s while recognizing that aviation, submarines, communications, and night operations had changed the problem inherited from the First World War. Exercises produced more questions and improvement points than grounds for confidence, even in areas such as night fighting where the service compared well with other navies. That willingness to expose uncertainty mattered because the fleet still had a decade to refine doctrine before the Second World War. The service benchmarked itself against whichever navy or formation seemed most capable and demanded further progress from officers and formations instead of treating competence as enough.

evidence.note: The transcript summarizes the exercises as preparation, experimentation, and continual self-comparison.

segments.summary: The closing assessment presents the exercises as a learning system that exposed uncertainty and demanded improvement a decade before the Second World War.
